channel.title: B.I.A.S.
channel.description: Balanced Information, Actual Stories. Biased toward calm.

item.title: Solar eclipse and the island of Ireland: The weather forecast and all you need to know
item.description:
Skywatchers across Ireland are preparing for a rare celestial treat: a deep partial solar eclipse on Wednesday that will obscure more than 90% of the sun—the most dramatic eclipse visible from the island until 2090. The timing is remarkable, as the eclipse will be followed just hours later by the peak of the Perseid meteor shower, creating what one astronomer describes as "celestial fireworks." For those traveling to Spain, a total eclipse lasting nearly two minutes awaits.
The eclipse will begin around 6:10 PM BST, with coverage varying by location. Belfast will see 93% of the sun covered, while Skellig Michael off the Kerry coast will experience nearly complete obscuration at 98%. Astronomers emphasize that even with such extensive coverage, the remaining sunlight remains dangerously bright—looking directly at it can damage the retina without any pain warning. Viewers are urged to use certified eclipse glasses or creative alternatives like pinhole viewers or even kitchen colanders to safely project the sun's image. The weather forecast offers mixed prospects, with cloud cover likely in parts of Northern Ireland while southern and eastern counties may enjoy clearer skies.
What makes this event quietly extraordinary is its rarity and the convergence of cosmic events in a single evening. For researchers like Ryan Milligan, who has traveled to Spain for his thirteenth eclipse, the experience transcends data and screens—it's described as visceral and emotional, a moment when day turns to night and the familiar world briefly transforms. For those staying home, even a partial eclipse offers a reminder of our place in a dynamic solar system, a spectacle that won't return in this form for seven decades.

item.title: Rare piglet the size of 'a grapefruit with legs' born at zoo
item.description:
A tiny babirusa piglet named Rana has made her public debut at Chester Zoo, offering a glimmer of hope for a species teetering on the brink of extinction. When she was born, keepers described her as roughly the size of a grapefruit with legs—a fitting image for one of nature's more unusual creatures. Babirusas, known as "pig-deer" in Malay due to their distinctive appearance, are found on only four Indonesian islands and face catastrophic decline in the wild, primarily due to African swine fever that reached their habitat five years ago.
Unlike most pigs, babirusas typically give birth to just one or two offspring at a time rather than large litters, making population recovery painfully slow. New mothers are also highly sensitive to disturbance, so keepers monitored Rana and her mother Matano remotely until they were ready for visitors. Matano herself was born at Chester Zoo eleven years ago and now has descendants across Europe, representing an important genetic safety net. The species, long classified as vulnerable, is being upgraded to critically endangered—a sobering reflection of how quickly their situation has deteriorated.
Beyond their quirky looks—males sport upper tusks that curve dramatically back toward their faces—babirusas play a crucial ecological role. As they forage, they disperse seeds that aid forest regeneration, making them vital to the health of island ecosystems. Conservationists describe Rana as a lifeline for her species and emphasize that her birth represents a race against time to prevent the loss of one of the oldest pig species still living. It's a quiet reminder that even the most charismatic and culturally significant creatures can vanish if we're not paying attention.

item.title: ‘It’s going to be spectacular’: Millions flock to Spain seeking best view of total solar eclipse
item.description:
Spain is preparing to host what may be one of the most-watched celestial events of the year: the country's first total solar eclipse in more than a century. A narrow band stretching roughly 200 kilometers from the northwest coast to Mallorca will experience totality on Wednesday, with officials estimating that up to 6 million people could gather along the path. While tens of millions across western Europe will witness a partial eclipse, Spain offers some of the best viewing conditions on mainland Europe, making it a magnet for eclipse chasers from around the world.
An estimated 460,000 visitors have traveled to Spain for the event, booking hotels months in advance and arriving from as far as Japan, the United States, and Canada. Among them is Angela Jones Rieksts from Halifax, who was moved to tears by her first total eclipse two years ago and now considers herself a devoted eclipse chaser. Preparations have been extensive: opticians and pharmacies sold out of eclipse glasses, Spanish airline Iberia organized a charter flight to view the phenomenon from 10,000 meters, and more than 24,000 police officers are being deployed to manage an expected 1.5 million additional car journeys. With temperatures forecast to reach 40°C and wildfire risks elevated, authorities are taking no chances.
This story captures a rare moment when millions pause to witness something larger than themselves—a celestial alignment that lasts less than two minutes but leaves lasting impressions. It's a reminder of how nature's grandest spectacles can still inspire awe, draw people across continents, and create shared experiences that transcend borders and everyday concerns.

item.title: Hiroshi Okuda, Toyota chair who pushed for the Prius, dies at 93
item.description:
Hiroshi Okuda, the visionary leader who guided Toyota Motor Corporation through a transformative period in the late 1990s and early 2000s, has passed away at 93. His tenure marked a significant shift for the Japanese automaker, as he became the first president from outside the founding family in a generation when he assumed the role in 1995.
Okuda's leadership style set him apart in Japan's often consensus-driven corporate culture. Tall, outspoken, and willing to take calculated risks, he pushed Toyota to embrace innovation at a time when the automotive industry stood on the cusp of major change. Under his guidance, the company launched the Prius, the pioneering gas-electric hybrid that would reshape global attitudes toward fuel efficiency and environmental responsibility in transportation. He also championed the RAV4 SUV, which became another commercial success. Beyond product development, Okuda earned recognition internally for his cost-cutting initiatives and decisive leadership, which he saw as essential antidotes to the bureaucratic inertia that can slow large corporations.
Okuda's career spanned the arc of Toyota's rise from a post-World War II manufacturer to a global automotive giant. His willingness to bet on unconventional technology like hybrid powertrains—when such vehicles were unproven in the marketplace—demonstrates a forward-thinking approach that helped position Toyota as an industry leader in sustainable transportation. This story reminds us how individual leadership and the courage to pursue untested ideas can shape entire industries and influence how millions of people move through the world.

item.title: UK to get best eclipse since 1999 as Moon blocks out Sun across Europe
item.description:
On Wednesday evening, the UK experienced its most significant solar eclipse since 1999—and the best the country will see for another half-century. Up to 96% of the Sun was covered by the Moon, with the peak occurring between 18:58 and 19:15 BST. Devon, Cornwall, and parts of Wales enjoyed the fullest views, while much of the country saw coverage exceeding 90%. Demand for eclipse glasses surged, with one London bakery selling around 100 pairs in a single morning.
Meanwhile, northern Spain, along with parts of Russia, Greenland, Iceland, and Portugal, witnessed a total eclipse. An estimated half a million visitors traveled to Spain for the event, gathering in cities like Bilbao, Valencia, and Palma to experience the minute and forty seconds of totality—when the Moon completely obscures the Sun and daylight briefly fades. Observers described the phenomenon as a chance to witness "the grandeur of nature," with families investing in the experience rather than "trivial things." Weather conditions were largely favorable across Spain, though some parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland faced cloudy skies.
Solar eclipses occur roughly every 18 months somewhere on Earth, but being in the path of totality—where the Moon's shadow falls—is rare for any given location. The UK won't see this level of coverage again until 2081, and a total eclipse won't grace British skies until 2090. For those fortunate enough to witness it, the event served as a humbling reminder of the celestial mechanics quietly unfolding above us, connecting strangers across continents in shared wonder.

item.title: 12yo will walk 500km for meeting with with prime minister in Canberra
item.description:
A twelve-year-old boy from Warren, a small town in western New South Wales, has decided to walk 500 kilometers to Australia's capital to advocate for better healthcare access for children in rural communities. Dusty Langby's ambitious 16-day trek to Parliament House isn't just symbolic—he's already raised $100,000 toward a $1 million goal for Little Wings, a charity that provides free flights to Sydney for rural children needing specialist care and brings pediatricians to remote communities.
The idea came to Dusty while swimming in his family's dam in January, a moment of inspiration that has since blossomed into a campaign with genuine impact. He and his brother have both benefited from Little Wings' services, being flown from Warren to Sydney for medical appointments, and Dusty wants other children to have the same opportunities. The funds he's raised so far can already provide a year of pediatric visits to five rural communities—care that would reach nearly 400 children. A team including the charity's CEO and local nurses will walk alongside him, and Dusty has secured something the organization itself never could: a meeting with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whom he plans to ask to match his fundraising total.
This story offers a quiet reminder that meaningful advocacy can come from anywhere, even from a twelve-year-old who's already worn through four pairs of training shoes. Dusty's determination highlights both the healthcare gaps facing rural Australia and the power of one person—however young—to mobilize attention and resources toward solving them.

item.title: Meet the Indigenous women restoring Kenya’s Mau Forest — and reshaping gender roles
item.description:
In the highlands of southwestern Kenya, a network of Indigenous women is quietly rewriting two stories at once: the future of the Mau Forest and their own roles within their communities. The Paran Women Group, founded in 2005, now connects 64 registered groups of mostly Maasai and Ogiek women across several counties. Through tree nurseries, beekeeping, kitchen gardens, and landscape restoration, these women are healing one of Kenya's most vital forest ecosystems while carving out new forms of independence and influence in their daily lives.
For many participants, the work represents a profound shift. Women like Judy Mukut balance conservation efforts with traditional domestic responsibilities—milking cattle, preparing meals, and caring for children—yet find time to gather at community resource centers where they raise seedlings, share ecological knowledge, and build new skills. Nancy Letina, who joined after her husband's death left her responsible for four children, describes how the program transformed her from complete economic dependence to self-sufficiency. Recent research supports this dual approach: a 2025 study found that restoration programs intentionally designed to address gender inequality not only empower women in household decision-making but also improve conservation outcomes over the long term.
This story matters because it illustrates how environmental restoration and social change can grow from the same soil. The women of Paran aren't waiting for permission or outside solutions—they're demonstrating that caring for forests and reshaping centuries-old gender roles can happen simultaneously, one seedling and one decision at a time.

item.title: A little-remembered Gilded Age millionaire helped make milk safe for American kids through his ‘retail giving’
item.description:
In a time when philanthropists like Rockefeller and Carnegie set sweeping goals to benefit all humanity, one wealthy businessman took a different path. Nathan Straus, co-owner of Macy's department store, focused his charitable energy on a modest but urgent problem: making milk safe for children to drink. His story, explored in Andrew Fisher's new biography, offers a compelling case for what might be called "retail giving"—philanthropy with humble, practical aims that can nonetheless save thousands of lives.
Straus came from a German Jewish family that immigrated to America in the 1850s. After establishing themselves in Georgia, the Civil War disrupted their business and pushed them north to New York City. There, the Straus brothers built a thriving business selling china and glassware, eventually partnering with and then fully acquiring Macy's during the retailing revolution of the late 19th century. While his brother Isidor managed store operations and another brother Oscar entered politics, Nathan handled external affairs and increasingly turned his attention to public health causes, particularly championing the pasteurization of milk at a time when contaminated dairy was a deadly threat to children.
This story matters because it quietly challenges our assumptions about effective philanthropy. While grand visions capture the history books, Straus demonstrated that targeting a single, solvable problem—ensuring children had access to safe milk—could create profound change. His approach stands as a reminder that transformative giving doesn't always require worldwide ambitions; sometimes the most meaningful impact comes from addressing the immediate, overlooked needs right in front of us.

item.title: Lebanon parliament votes to end death penalty, 1st in Middle East to do so
item.description:
Lebanon has become the first country in the Middle East to formally abolish the death penalty, with parliament voting to replace capital punishment with life imprisonment and aggravated hard labor. The decision transforms what had been an unofficial moratorium on executions—in place since 2004—into permanent legal protection. At the time of the vote, 85 people were facing death sentences in Lebanon.
The legislation passed with majority support in the 128-member assembly, though Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc opposed the measure. Justice Minister Adel Nassar called it a "historic step," and human rights organizations praised the move as a significant milestone for the region. Amnesty International noted that Lebanon is now aligned with a global trend toward abolition, turning a temporary pause in executions into lasting human rights progress. However, practical questions remain about how the new punishment of aggravated hard labor will actually be enforced, given Lebanon's resource constraints and overcrowded prisons.
The timing is complex: parliament is simultaneously debating a broad amnesty law that could reduce sentences or release individuals convicted of violent offenses—the largest such amnesty since Lebanon's civil war ended in 1990. This has drawn protests from families of victims, some of whom had hoped to see perpetrators executed rather than granted reduced sentences. The story offers a window into how societies navigate competing values around justice, mercy, and human rights, even amid practical challenges and deep disagreements about what accountability should look like.

item.title: Lunar calendar: Mayan book predicted eclipses a thousand years ago
item.description:
A thousand years ago, Maya astronomers created something that continues to astonish modern scientists: a lunar calendar so precise it could predict solar eclipses across centuries. The Dresden Codex, one of the oldest surviving books in the Americas, contains an intricate system that tracked the moon's cycles and anticipated eclipses with remarkable accuracy—all without telescopes, computers, or modern physics.
What makes this achievement particularly impressive is how the Maya solved a problem that plagues all lunar calendars: the moon's cycles don't align perfectly with solar years, causing errors to accumulate over time. The Maya developed what researchers now recognize as a kind of ancestral "algorithmic thinking," creating a system that combined different lunar cycles and included periodic corrections to keep the calendar synchronized. Through patient observation spanning generations and ingenious calculations, they built a tool that could forecast virtually every solar eclipse visible from Maya territories between 350 and 1150 CE, with an error margin of only about one hour.
This story offers a quiet reminder of the sophistication of ancient scientific thinking. The Dresden Codex reveals a culture deeply invested in understanding celestial patterns, not through sudden flashes of genius, but through methodical observation, careful record-keeping, and mathematical innovation passed down across generations. It's a testament to what human curiosity and persistence can achieve, even without the technology we now take for granted.

item.title: ‘I feel motherly towards them’: the nature reserve manager sharing her office with a wasp nest
item.description:
When a wasp colony moved into Eilish Rothney's office at a Norfolk nature reserve, her initial impulse to remove them gave way to curiosity. The reserve manager decided to share her workspace with the expanding nest, which now towers over a metre tall and blankets an entire bookshelf in intricate layers of chewed wood pulp. What began as an unwelcome intrusion became an unexpected cohabitation experiment.
Rothney adapted her routine to accommodate her new officemates, opening a window to give them a clear flight path and moving calmly through the space. She describes the nest as almost a living organism itself, emitting a low purring sound from thousands of wings beating to regulate temperature. Her observations reveal the colony's remarkable dynamics: a queen laying eggs continuously, workers foraging and feeding larvae, and a complex exchange of nutrients that keeps the system running. Rather than fear stings, Rothney believes insects recognize individuals who mean them no harm, advocating for calm coexistence.
Her tolerance extends beyond her own office to defending the wasps that crash summer picnics. She explains that late-summer aggression stems from desperation—adult workers suddenly cut off from their main food source when larvae stop producing sugary secretions. As autumn approaches and the colony's natural lifecycle winds down, Rothney admits she'll feel motherly sadness when her temporary colleagues depart. This quiet story matters because it challenges our reflexive hostility toward creatures we've labeled pests, suggesting that understanding and patience might replace convenience-driven extermination. It's a gentle reminder that coexistence, even with wasps, is often more rewarding than we imagine.

item.title: First in her family to speak English, Brazilian overcomes competition from 33,000 candidates and wins World Bank internship
item.description:
Gabrielle Hayashi Santos, a young woman from Bauru in the interior of São Paulo, Brazil, has achieved something quietly extraordinary: securing one of 120 internship positions at the World Bank, competing against nearly 33,000 candidates. What makes her story particularly striking is that she's the first in her family to speak English, earn a postgraduate degree, or study abroad—milestones born from determination rather than privilege.
Growing up, international exchanges seemed impossibly distant. Her father left school in elementary grades to work various jobs—collecting cans, driving trucks, working as a mechanic—only completing high school when Gabrielle was six. Her mother, a pharmacist of Japanese descent, moved from a small agricultural town in Mato Grosso to attend university. The family's only connection to the world beyond Brazil was relatives traveling to Japan for factory work to send money home. Yet Gabrielle discovered through persistent research that scholarships could open doors she'd assumed were closed. Starting in high school, she won funding for courses abroad in leadership and entrepreneurship. Her mother initially worried the opportunities might be scams, but gradually came to trust the programs. Gabrielle went on to study International Relations, complete a master's in Germany, and intern at UNESCO, focusing on how careers can transform not just individuals but entire families.
Her story offers something worth pausing over: a reminder that ambitious paths aren't reserved for those born into them. Gabrielle's achievement isn't just about personal success—it's about expanding what seems possible, one generation opening doors the previous couldn't have imagined, and the quiet persistence required to cross thresholds that once seemed firmly shut.

item.title: Three sports groups using movement to tackle isolation
item.description:
Three grassroots organizations are demonstrating how physical activity can become a bridge out of loneliness and isolation, offering something deeper than conventional fitness programs. Sport in Mind, founded in 2010 to help one unwell friend, has now supported more than 60,000 people experiencing mental health challenges through free sessions ranging from football and walking to gardening and dance. Rather than emphasizing competition, the charity works with the NHS and community partners to create welcoming environments where movement becomes a pathway to routine, confidence, and recovery.
The Bluetits Chill Swimmers takes a different approach, building a global volunteer-led community around cold water swimming and dipping. What started in Wales has expanded into informal local groups where the focus isn't endurance or performance, but the simple pleasure of being in nature together, gently challenging oneself, and finding companionship through shared ritual. Meanwhile, GoodGym combines exercise with practical community service, connecting runners, walkers, and cyclists with local projects and isolated older people who need help with tasks like garden clearing or home projects.
What makes these initiatives quietly remarkable is their recognition that movement doesn't have to be solitary or competitive to be valuable. By weaving physical activity together with connection, purpose, and service, they're transforming exercise from an individual pursuit into something that strengthens entire communities while addressing the very real challenges of loneliness and mental health that many people face today.

item.title: To No Longer Bow Our Heads: Searching for the Disappeared of the Spanish Civil War (3/4)
item.description:
Ninety years after the Spanish Civil War began, thousands of families are still searching for their missing loved ones. More than 100,000 people remain unidentified, the vast majority victims of Francoist repression. Recent excavations are finally allowing descendants to recover remains and provide dignified burials—bringing closure to wounds that have spanned generations.
The story of Antonio Carrascal Lema illustrates this long journey toward peace. An agricultural worker and municipal councilor affiliated with the socialist workers' union, he was executed by rebel forces in September 1936. For ninety years, his granddaughter Adela knew little about his fate. The trauma ran deep, silenced by pain and official obstruction—when the family sought information, they were told archives had been burned. In 2024, a phone call changed everything: excavations in Zufre's cemetery uncovered nine bodies, and DNA testing with Antonio's still-living daughter confirmed his identity. "He now rests in peace. We have triumphed over forgetting," Adela said at the May 2026 ceremony where she finally laid him to rest beside his wife.
The Spanish Civil War claimed at least 500,000 lives between 1936 and 1939, with repercussions lasting until 1948. While bodies of those executed by Republicans were exhumed and returned to families after the war, Francoist victims were left in unmarked graves and mass burial sites. This story matters because it reveals how historical wounds persist across generations when truth remains buried, and how the simple act of knowing—of finally being able to name and honor the dead—can bring dignity back to families who were forced to bow their heads for far too long.

item.title: Perseid meteor shower reaches peak: When and where to catch a glimpse
item.description:
The Perseids meteor shower, widely considered the best annual celestial display, reaches its peak this week, offering skywatchers a chance to see up to 100 shooting stars per hour. This year brings an unusual bonus: a deep partial solar eclipse visible in the UK will occur just hours before the meteor shower begins, creating what astronomer Dr. Becky Smethurst calls "the perfect cosmic coincidence of events." The Perseids are caused by debris from the Swift-Tuttle comet, a massive object with a 16-mile solid core that takes 133 years to orbit the Sun, meaning some of the burning fragments may have been left behind more than a century ago.
While the Perseids are active from mid-July through late August, the prime viewing window falls in the early morning hours of August 12-13, between midnight and dawn. This year offers especially favorable conditions due to the new moon, which means no competing moonlight to wash out fainter meteors. For the best experience, observers should seek locations away from city lights, allow their eyes 20-30 minutes to adjust to darkness, and look toward the widest possible expanse of sky. England and Wales are expected to have clear skies, while Scotland and Northern Ireland may contend with more cloud cover.
This story offers a gentle reminder to look up and reconnect with the cosmos. The Perseids provide a rare chance to witness ancient debris burning up in real time, connecting us to celestial events that unfold on timescales far beyond human lifespans—what Smethurst aptly describes as "the Universe's own cosmic clock."

item.title: Indigenous artist travels 600 km to exhibit Karipuna body art at Amapá Expo: 'Representing my people is priceless'
item.description:
A 28-year-old Karipuna artist traveled more than 600 kilometers from his indigenous territory in Brazil's far north to share his people's traditional body art at a cultural exposition in Macapá. Eddír Iaparrá Karipuna's journey from the Uaçá Indigenous Land in Oiapoque required long hours by road and river, but for him, the opportunity to represent his community carried meaning beyond measure.
At the Expofeira 2026, Eddír paints traditional geometric patterns on visitors' skin using natural ink made from genipap fruit and charcoal. Each design carries ancestral significance—the spiral, for example, serves as a protective amulet against negative energy. For indigenous peoples, these body graphics function as a visual language expressing identity, spirituality, and connection to nature, acting both as markers of belonging and symbolic shields. The experience draws curious visitors, including a tourist from Pernambuco who had always wanted body art but feared needles, and found the temporary natural ink painting a beautiful alternative.
The artist, who is also a musician and composer, emphasizes that his presence represents countless community members who couldn't make the difficult journey. The indigenous pavilion at the free nine-day exposition features representatives from seven Amapá ethnic groups, showcasing feather earrings, natural accessories, and handcrafted objects. This story quietly illuminates how cultural traditions traverse distance and time, finding new audiences while maintaining their sacred meanings—a reminder that preservation and sharing need not be contradictory, and that sometimes the greatest honor lies simply in showing up for one's people.

item.title: Jackie, a beloved bald eagle and livestream star, dies of mysterious illness
item.description:
Jackie, a bald eagle who became an unlikely internet sensation through a livestream of her nest at California's Big Bear Lake, has died at age 14 from an unidentified illness. The eagle had been receiving care at the Ojai Raptor Center since mid-July, when she was found weak and unable to fly following an altercation with younger eagles. Despite extensive testing including CT scans and bone marrow biopsies, veterinary experts were unable to determine the cause of her severe anemia.
Millions of viewers worldwide had followed Jackie's life since the livestream began in 2015, initially watching her parents before Jackie herself took over the nest in 2018. Her partnership with Shadow, her mate, became particularly popular during the pandemic as audiences watched them raise multiple clutches of chicks. This year brought both heartbreak and joy: ravens consumed their first two eggs in January, but Jackie laid replacements in February, successfully hatching Luna and Sandy. The latter was named in honor of a recently deceased conservationist.
Jackie's influence extended far beyond entertainment. Her presence sparked a remarkable $10 million conservation effort by Friends of Big Bear Lake to purchase 63 acres near her nest that had been threatened by development. The campaign drew support from local schoolchildren to tech entrepreneurs, demonstrating how a single wild creature can galvanize environmental action. Jackie's story reminds us that sometimes the most powerful conservation ambassadors are simply living their lives while we watch—and in watching, we learn to care deeply about protecting the wild spaces they call home.

item.title: Yarning circles raise concerns about repetition of Stolen Generations
item.description:
In South Australia, nearly 40 percent of children in out-of-home care are Aboriginal, despite Aboriginal people making up a small fraction of the population. Carers and community members are raising alarm that this disproportionate representation echoes the trauma of the Stolen Generations, particularly as many children are losing connection to their culture, language, and land. South Australia has the second-highest rate of children in out-of-home care nationally, and Aboriginal children there are placed in care at a rate significantly higher than the national average.
An Aboriginal-led organization called KWY has launched a four-year research project, Wilto Willo—meaning "spring star" in the Kaurna language—to gather community voices and develop solutions. Through yarning circles in Port Lincoln, Port Augusta, and Adelaide, about 200 carers have shared their experiences. They report systemic issues including high staff turnover, fly-in fly-out workers, long waits for medical and psychological assessments, and a failure to follow Aboriginal placement principles, which prioritize keeping children connected to family and culture. Some children have gone six months without a support worker, and many have been placed in non-Indigenous homes where they've had little opportunity to learn their heritage or visit country.
This story matters because it highlights an urgent question: despite policies aimed at closing the gap and protecting Aboriginal children's rights, why are the numbers worsening? The research suggests that most child protection funding goes toward intervening after harm, rather than preventing it. By centering Aboriginal voices and community-led solutions, Wilto Willo offers a path forward—one that honors identity, belonging, and the hard lessons of history.

item.title: Quitting dream job over climate fears a 'no-brainer' for former pilot
item.description:
After four decades as a commercial pilot and 25,000 hours in the sky, Geoff Collis made an unexpected career change driven by climate concerns. The former Jetstar pilot, who fell in love with aviation at age ten, found himself increasingly troubled by the environmental cost of his dream job—ordering 2.4 million liters of jet fuel annually. When COVID-19 grounded much of the industry, the then-55-year-old began an apprenticeship at a local Melbourne bakery, discovering unexpected fulfillment in the craft of bread and pastry making.
Though he briefly returned to flying in 2023 when the aviation sector recovered, Collis ultimately decided he could no longer reconcile his work with his climate conscience. He described much of the industry's environmental efforts as "tokenism, spin and greenwashing," making his departure feel inevitable. Aviation presents a unique environmental challenge: while responsible for only two to three percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, it's one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize. The International Civil Aviation Organization projects emissions could increase two to five times 2018 levels by 2070, even as other industries reduce their carbon footprints. Airlines like Qantas acknowledge operating on growth models while investing in sustainable aviation fuel and newer aircraft.
This story resonates because it captures a deeply personal response to a global dilemma—what happens when passion and principle collide? Collis's choice represents the kind of difficult reckoning many may face as climate realities deepen, and his transition from cockpit to kitchen suggests that meaningful work can be found in unexpected places, even when it means leaving behind the dream of a lifetime.

item.title: Measles returns to spark alert in Brazil: who needs to get vaccinated? See questions and answers about the disease
item.description:
Brazil is experiencing a renewed measles alert, with 24 confirmed cases reported as of early February—23 in São Paulo state and one in Rio de Janeiro. The resurgence comes amid a broader measles outbreak across the Americas, including the largest surge in the United States in 35 years. Health experts point to declining vaccination rates, fueled partly by misinformation and anti-vaccine movements, as the primary reason the virus has regained a foothold in communities with insufficient immunity.
Brazil only recently regained its measles elimination certification in 2024, and while the current case count is far lower than outbreaks in other countries, officials are taking the situation seriously. The cases have been traced to imported infections, many linked to international travel, including Brazilians returning from the World Cup in countries with higher case numbers. In response, cities like São Paulo, Guarulhos, and São Bernardo do Campo are offering measles vaccines to everyone aged six months to 59 years, regardless of vaccination history, to break potential transmission chains.
The story offers a window into how infectious diseases respect no borders and how quickly progress can be reversed without vigilant public health measures. Measles is not a mild illness—it spreads with remarkable ease, and the virus can cause serious complications affecting the lungs and nervous system. As international travel rebounds, this quiet alarm in Brazil underscores the importance of maintaining high vaccination coverage to protect communities and preserve hard-won public health achievements.

item.title: Dogs can distinguish between fearful and angry or sad human faces, brain scans suggest
item.description:
Dogs may be more attuned to human emotions than previously understood. New research using brain imaging has revealed that canine brains can distinguish not only between happy and unhappy human faces, but also between different types of negative expressions—a ability researchers say represents the first demonstration that dogs can differentiate emotions of the same emotional valence.
In the study, researchers at the University of Vienna trained pet dogs to lie still in MRI scanners while viewing photographs of unfamiliar human faces displaying various emotions. Initial experiments showed increased brain activity in areas associated with visual processing, social cognition, and reward when dogs viewed happy faces compared to neutral ones. A second experiment involving twelve dogs and four different expressions—happiness, sadness, fear, and anger—revealed something more nuanced: while certain brain regions could distinguish happy from any negative expression, distinguishing between different unhappy faces required analyzing activity across the entire brain. The dogs' brains could tell fearful faces apart from angry or sad ones, though anger and sadness proved harder to differentiate from each other. Researchers suggest this may reflect how different negative expressions signal different types of threats, and that dogs might need additional cues like body language to make finer distinctions.
This research offers a window into how thousands of years of domestication have shaped dogs' remarkable sensitivity to human communication. Beyond satisfying curiosity about our companions' inner lives, the findings suggest practical applications—such as using positive facial expressions to enhance training—and remind us that the bond between humans and dogs runs deeper than we might see on the surface.

item.title: In Côte d'Ivoire, biama has all the youth dancing
item.description:
In the bustling streets of Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire, a new dance and music phenomenon has captured the hearts of young people across the nation. Born just five years ago in Yopougon—the city's poorest yet most vibrant district—biama has become a cultural force that speaks to a generation. The style pulses with energy, moving even faster than coupé-décalé, an earlier Ivorian genre known for its association with glamorous nightclubs and flashy displays.
What sets biama apart is its accessibility and democratic spirit. While coupé-décalé belonged to exclusive nightclub culture, biama thrives in open spaces—street corners, public squares, and smartphone screens. Young dancers, known as biamasseurs, share their moves on TikTok and other social platforms, building vast audiences without the backing of traditional record labels. The most popular performers have achieved remarkable success, amassing millions of views online and embarking on tours across Europe and Africa, all while staying rooted in the grassroots culture that birthed the movement.
This story offers a window into how creativity flourishes in unexpected places and how digital platforms have reshaped the landscape of cultural expression. Biama represents more than just dance steps and rhythms; it's a testament to young people claiming public space, building community, and creating opportunities outside conventional industry structures. In a world often focused on top-down cultural production, here's a movement rising from the streets, connecting a generation through joy, movement, and shared identity.

item.title: August will have two eclipses, but only one can be seen from Brazil
item.description:
August brings a rare celestial double feature: two eclipses within the same month, each visible from different parts of the world. While a total solar eclipse will grace the Northern Hemisphere on August 12th, it's the second event—a partial lunar eclipse on August 28th—that will capture the attention of skywatchers across Brazil and much of the Americas, Europe, and Africa.
The solar eclipse occurs when the Moon positions itself precisely between the Sun and Earth, casting its shadow across the planet. This month's total eclipse will trace a path across Greenland, Iceland, northern Russia, Spain, and a small portion of Portugal, with partial views available across much of Europe. Unfortunately for South American observers, the phenomenon won't be visible at all from Brazil. But the lunar eclipse later in the month offers everyone a chance to participate. Beginning at 1 a.m. local time on August 28th, the event will be visible to the naked eye throughout all Brazilian states, requiring no special equipment or travel to remote viewing locations.
This story reminds us that the universe operates on its own schedule, occasionally offering us two celestial performances in a single month. While one eclipse passes by unseen, the other arrives as an invitation—a chance to look up in the predawn darkness and witness Earth's shadow gently crossing the Moon's face, connecting observers across continents in a shared moment of wonder.

item.title: Boa constrictor rescued by firefighters from inside speaker in Ceará; video
item.description:
In the coastal town of Aracati, Brazil, a couple transporting sound equipment for their evangelical band made an unexpected discovery: a boa constrictor had taken up residence inside one of their speakers. The mystery began when the husband noticed something shifting inside the equipment during transport last Saturday. What should have been routine setup for a performance turned into a curious wildlife encounter.
When a sound technician opened the speaker cabinet at the couple's shop, he found the snake coiled inside the speaker housing. Rather than attempt removal themselves, the owners wisely contacted local firefighters, who safely extracted the serpent without harm to animal or humans. The most puzzling aspect of the situation remains unsolved: no one knows how the boa entered the equipment, when it arrived, or how long it had been living there. According to owner Valéria Vilck, the speaker had been in regular use, vibrating with music while its stowaway remained hidden and undetected.
This story offers a gentle reminder of how wildlife and human spaces intersect in unexpected ways, even in the most unlikely places. There's something quietly remarkable about a snake finding shelter in an instrument meant to amplify sound, surviving unnoticed amid the very vibrations that might have driven other creatures away. It's a small tale that speaks to both the adaptability of nature and the importance of responding to such surprises with care rather than panic.

item.title: Rare visitor: only semi-albino female southern right whale recorded since 1987 sighted in Santa Catarina; VIDEO
item.description:
Off the coast of Santa Catarina, Brazil, researchers have documented a remarkable return visitor: the only known semi-albino female southern right whale recorded in the country since cataloging began in 1987. The whale, designated B-964, was first identified in August 2023 swimming with her calf near the beaches of Garopaba and Imbituba. Her distinctive gray skin marked with black patches makes her unmistakable among her species.
Semi-albinism is exceptionally rare in southern right whales, occurring in only about 3% of individuals worldwide. Of the 38 semi-albino whales documented in Brazil's photo-identification catalog over nearly four decades, B-964 is the sole female. The coloration results from a recessive genetic variation—both parents must carry the gene for a semi-albino calf to be born. These whales are born white and gradually develop their characteristic gray coloring as they mature. When B-964 was spotted again in July 2024, she was swimming alone in waters known as a natural nursery for the species. Researchers suspect she may have returned to give birth, as southern right whales typically bear calves every three years.
This story offers a quiet window into the careful, patient work of marine conservation. The researchers' hope to spot B-964 with a new calf reflects decades of dedication to understanding individual whales through distinctive physical markers like head callosities and body patterns. It's a reminder that even among creatures as vast and ancient as whales, individuals matter—and that persistence in observation can reveal the exceptional hidden within the everyday rhythms of migration and reproduction.

item.title: Real estate agent offers to repair 20 public housing homes for free
item.description:
A Canberra real estate agent who once experienced homelessness himself is mobilizing an unusual solution to a troubling gap in public housing. Jonny Warren, who lived on the streets as a teenager while struggling with addiction, has launched a campaign to repair 20 vacant government-owned homes before Christmas—all pro bono. His motivation came from a visceral encounter during a charity patrol: seeing a mother and her four-year-old sleeping in a car.
The numbers behind Warren's initiative highlight a frustrating paradox. More than 580 public housing properties sit empty in the Australian Capital Territory, with 285 requiring repairs before they can welcome tenants. Meanwhile, over 3,650 approved applicants languish on the waiting list—some for more than five years. Warren has already assembled a volunteer army of tradespeople ready to tackle the work, which ranges from deep cleaning to installing new carpets and fixtures. He describes many of the properties as needing only "final little touches" rather than major overhauls.
While housing advocates welcome the effort, they caution that dignified, quality repairs require more than quick fixes. Independent legislator Thomas Emerson is backing the plan and pressing the government to support it, calling the vacancy situation "insane" amid such acute need. Warren's story illustrates how personal experience can spark creative community action, while also raising questions about why systemic gaps persist when willing hands are ready to help. It's a reminder that sometimes the resources to solve a problem are already present—they just need coordination and permission to act.

item.title: Italy’s record-low Po River forces farmers to weigh crop switch
item.description:
Italy's Po River, the lifeblood of the country's industrial heartland, is swinging between devastating extremes as climate change disrupts centuries of predictable water supply. The 652-kilometer waterway, which rises in the Alps and flows to the Adriatic, supports nearly 41% of Italy's GDP and a third of its agricultural output. Now, farmers like Massimo Salvagnin face an unsettling calculation: whether planting seeds will result in crops or simply cook them in superheated soil.
The river recently fell to a record low at Cremona, dropping below even the severe 2022 drought mark, with flow reduced to less than a third of normal levels. Yet the challenge isn't only drought. Spring snowmelt can send 10 billion cubic meters of water past Ferrara in under two weeks, while months later the same region scrambles for every drop. Infrastructure manager Stefano Calderoni operates 4,200 kilometers of canals and 160 pumps to manage farmland reclaimed from marshes, much of it below sea level. The system was designed for nature's predictable rhythms, not today's volatile swings between flood and drought.
This story offers a window into how climate change is quietly rewriting the rules for regions built on assumptions of stability. It's not about distant projections or abstract models, but about a farmer standing in his field, seeds in hand, forced to gamble on whether the ground itself has become too hostile for life to take root. The Po's transformation speaks to a broader question facing communities everywhere: how to adapt systems designed for one climate reality to survive in another.

item.title: After decades of pleas, fallen miners from a historic mine will be memorialised
item.description:
In the outback Queensland town of Mount Isa, a long-awaited memorial will finally honor 151 miners who lost their lives at the historic mine that has defined the community for over a century. After nearly three decades of advocacy led by families and former residents, the $4.7 million landmark will overlook the mines from Frank Aston Hill, with completion expected by late 2027. The project brings together the state government, mining company Glencore, and local council in a shared commitment to remembrance.
The memorial holds deep personal significance for families like Steve Trevor's, who lost his brother Tony in a 1995 mining accident. Trevor describes memories that remain sharp nearly thirty years later—the midnight phone call, the ripple of grief through his family. Former resident John Moran, who first called for the memorial in 1998, emphasized that these workers were true residents of Mount Isa, embedded in the community rather than transient workers. The project had stalled despite plans being drawn up in 2023, until the current government repurposed funds originally designated for the region's economic transition following the copper mine's closure.
What makes this story quietly powerful is how it reveals the patient determination of a community insisting that sacrifice be acknowledged. The memorial serves multiple purposes: a place for families to grieve, a reminder of mining's human cost, and an educational touchstone for future generations. As Glencore's Troy Wilson noted, it will stand as both tribute and responsibility—honoring those who didn't come home while reinforcing the commitment to ensure today's workers do. It's a story about memory, community persistence, and the recognition that some debts take decades to properly honor.

item.title: First 500 schools to benefit from Solar in Schools programme announced
item.description:
New Zealand has announced the first 500 schools that will receive solar panel installations through its Solar in Schools programme, a $30 million initiative aimed at reducing energy costs and emissions. The selection includes 340 schools in the North Island, 157 in the South Island, and three in the Chatham Islands, with installations scheduled to roll out over the next three years.
The schools were chosen based on specific energy challenges: they're either experiencing energy insecurity, facing higher-than-average power costs, scheduled to replace aging gas or diesel boilers, or need improved energy resilience. Energy Minister Simeon Brown and Education Minister Erica Stanford unveiled the programme details at Te Papapa School in Auckland, emphasizing the dual benefits of generating clean energy while cutting operational costs. Large schools are expected to save approximately $8,000 annually on electricity bills by generating power from their rooftops rather than drawing exclusively from the grid.
This story matters because it represents a practical intersection of environmental action and community support. By installing solar panels on school buildings, the programme addresses immediate financial pressures on educational institutions while building renewable energy infrastructure where it can benefit young people directly. The initiative also promises to support regional businesses and help develop local solar industry expertise, creating ripple effects beyond the schoolyard fence. It's a reminder that climate solutions can be quietly pragmatic—reducing both carbon emissions and budget strain in one carefully planned move.

item.title: Divers find Roman ship over 2,000 years old off the coast of Sicily
item.description:
Off the western coast of Sicily, a local fisherman and diver named Giacomo De Mola recently stumbled upon what he initially thought was just another rock on the seafloor. Swimming closer through murky water at a depth of 46 meters, he realized he was looking at something far more remarkable: hundreds of ancient amphoras resting silently on the seabed. Italian authorities have confirmed the discovery of a Roman shipwreck estimated to be at least 2,100 years old, dating somewhere between the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE. The vessel, found roughly three nautical miles from the town of Mazara del Vallo, measures about 21 meters long and 6 meters wide.
The wreck is laden with ceramic jars—primarily Dressel 1A amphoras, tall cylindrical vessels typically used for transporting wine—as well as Lamboglia 2 amphoras likely originating from North Africa and a neo-Punic amphora. Italy's Ministry of Culture has classified the site as a significant underwater archaeological discovery, and regional authorities will continue detailed analysis to uncover more about the ship's story and cargo. Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli noted that the Mediterranean continues to reveal precious fragments of history, offering glimpses into the peoples, trade routes, and exchanges that made the sea a crossroads of civilizations.
This discovery matters because it offers a tangible link to the commercial networks that stitched together the ancient Mediterranean world. The quiet persistence of these artifacts, sleeping beneath the waves for over two millennia, reminds us that history often rests just beyond our everyday view, waiting for a curious eye and a moment of clarity to bring it back to light.

item.title: Perseid meteor shower set to dazzle northern hemisphere this week
item.description:
The Perseid meteor shower returns this week with particularly favorable viewing conditions across the northern hemisphere. The annual celestial display is expected to peak Wednesday night into Thursday morning, with astronomers predicting between 30 and 100 meteors per hour visible under ideal conditions. This year's show arrives with a bonus: it coincides with a total solar eclipse across Spain, Iceland, and Greenland, as well as a six-planet parade in the sky.
The Perseids occur when Earth passes through the debris trail left by comet Swift-Tuttle, an icy visitor that orbits the sun every 133 years and won't return until 2125. Observations of this particular meteor shower stretch back more than two millennia, making it one of humanity's oldest recorded sky-watching traditions. The Perseids have earned a special place among stargazers for producing brilliant fireballs and for arriving during warm summer months, sparing observers the discomfort of winter cold. This year's new moon phase adds another advantage—without bright moonlight washing out the sky, more meteors will be visible to patient observers.
This story offers a gentle reminder to look up from our screens and reconnect with the night sky. Astronomers recommend heading outside after dark, away from city lights, and allowing your eyes thirty minutes to adjust to the darkness. There's something quietly profound about witnessing debris from a distant comet colliding with our atmosphere at extraordinary speeds, creating streaks of light that have captivated humans for thousands of years. It's a cosmic spectacle that requires no special equipment, just curiosity and a patch of dark sky.

item.title: Father's Day: A story of love, grief, and new beginnings in Volta Redonda
item.description:
In Volta Redonda, Brazil, a father's journey through grief has blossomed into a story of resilience and renewed family bonds. Marcos became a father at 47, fulfilling a lifelong dream, but when his daughter Lara was just five years old, his wife died from metastatic breast cancer. Suddenly alone, he faced the daunting task of raising a young girl by himself, learning to navigate unfamiliar territory—from styling her hair to managing the emotional weight of being both father and mother.
The challenges were significant, but Marcos met them with quiet determination. Lara, now 11, speaks of her father with deep admiration, calling him her friend, her pride, and the person who "overcame everything" to care for her. Their bond, forged through loss and daily devotion, became the foundation of their small household. Then came another chapter: Rosângela entered their lives and embraced Lara with immediate maternal love, proving that families can be rebuilt and expanded through compassion and care.
This story resonates because it strips away the performative aspects of parenthood and reveals what remains: the unglamorous, transformative work of showing up each day. It's a reminder that love isn't static—it adapts, it grows, and sometimes it arrives when least expected, filling spaces we thought might stay empty forever.

item.title: Parnaíba turns 182: discover the architecture, landscapes and traditional cuisine of the city
item.description:
The coastal city of Parnaíba in Brazil's Piauí state recently celebrated its 182nd anniversary with a showcase of what makes the community special: historic architecture, dramatic natural landscapes, and traditional coastal cuisine. A local television program created a tour highlighting the city's cultural and environmental treasures, from colonial-era churches to the unique geography of the Parnaíba Delta.
Three historic churches anchor the city's architectural heritage. The Cathedral of Nossa Senhora Mãe da Divina Graça sits in the traditional town square, its history intertwined with the city's founding. The 18th-century Church of Nossa Senhora do Rosário holds particular significance as a space built for enslaved Black populations, preserving an important part of the region's social history. The Ermida de Nossa Senhora do Monte Serrat, constructed in 1711 when only eight houses existed nearby, stands as one of the municipality's oldest structures. Beyond the historic center, the Parnaíba Delta offers a contrasting landscape where rivers, mangroves, and dunes meet. Boat tours navigate channels between Piauí and Maranhão states, stopping at scenic points like Morro do Gavião, where visitors climb dunes for panoramic views. The Pedra do Sal beach features distinctive rock formations that divide the shore into calm and rough water sections, holding memories for longtime residents like 89-year-old Alaíde Sousa. The region's culinary identity centers on crab, a traditional ingredient that connects food to place.
This story offers a gentle reminder that a community's identity lives in the relationship between its past and present—in buildings that witnessed centuries of change, landscapes that shape daily life, and flavors that anchor people to home.

item.title: Who was Estevanico, the African slave who became the first great explorer of the current U.S.
item.description:
In 1528, a Moroccan man named Estevanico washed ashore on the coast of what is now Texas, barely alive after drifting across the Gulf of Mexico on a makeshift raft. He was one of only four survivors from a Spanish expedition of roughly 600 men that had set sail to conquer Florida and the Gulf Coast. Over the following years, this enslaved man would become the de facto leader of the small group and accomplish one of history's most remarkable survival journeys—yet his true name remains unknown to us.
Between 1528 and 1536, Estevanico walked approximately 3,620 kilometers westward from Florida to Mexico's Pacific coast, completing what is widely considered the first recorded crossing of North America and the Caribbean, nearly three centuries before the Lewis and Clark expedition. Along the way, he was captured by Native Americans, learned their languages, and became a healer. He later undertook an independent 2,400-kilometer journey northward, becoming the first known non-Native person to explore present-day New Mexico and Arizona. Despite being forbidden to travel to the New World as a Muslim, Estevanico pioneered routes and generated geographical knowledge that later Spanish explorers would use.
This story matters because it challenges familiar narratives about who first explored the American West. As the United States marks its 250th anniversary, a growing number of museums, tours, and monuments are finally highlighting Estevanico's previously overlooked legacy. His extraordinary journey reminds us that history's most significant pathfinders don't always appear in the expected chapters of our textbooks—and that courage and resilience can emerge from the most unlikely circumstances.

item.title: ‘Panda of the insect world’: the moscardón bumblebee creates buzz for invertebrate of the year
item.description:
In the temperate forests of Patagonia, a giant ginger bumblebee affectionately called the "flying mouse" is capturing hearts and concern. Bombus dahlbomii, the world's largest bumblebee species, boasts gloriously furry females that can reach 4cm in length and weigh up to 1.5g. These remarkable insects have evolved a special ability to see red flowers—a color most bees avoid—making them crucial pollinators for native Patagonian plants like the Chilean bellflower.
Despite their charm and ecological importance, these magnificent bumbles face a crisis not of their own making. Since the 1980s, two European bumblebee species were imported to Chile for commercial pollination. These non-native bees have spread rapidly, outcompeting the moscardón for resources while introducing pathogens that are devastating native populations. The ripple effects extend beyond the bees themselves: endemic mites that depend on Bombus dahlbomii are disappearing, while invasive European plants now benefit from the foreign pollinators. Researcher Anton Gradišek, who has studied these bees in the field and seen only a handful, calls them "the pandas of the insect world."
This story matters because it illustrates how well-intentioned human interventions can unravel delicate ecological relationships. The moscardón's plight is a quiet but urgent reminder that even helpful species become harmful when removed from their native contexts, and that some conservation mistakes cannot be easily undone. It's a call to consider the unseen connections that sustain biodiversity—and what we risk losing when we don't.

item.title: Total solar eclipse: Avellanosa de Muñó, the small Spanish village that for one night will be one of the most fascinating places on the planet
item.description:
In the heart of Spain's Burgos province lies Avellanosa de Muñó, a drowsy hamlet where the loudest sounds are bumblebees humming through lavender and the weekly bread van winding through empty streets. With no restaurants, no shops, and a bar that never opens, this village of fewer than a dozen permanent residents seems defined by absence. Yet on August 12, 2026, it will become one of the most captivating places on Earth.
A total solar eclipse will sweep across the Atlantic that evening, marking the first visible from mainland Europe since 1999 and from peninsular Spain since 1912. Avellanosa de Muñó sits directly in the narrow path of totality, offering golden wheat fields, low hills, and an unobstructed western horizon with minimal light pollution. The timing adds magic: occurring just before sunset, the eclipse will create a double twilight effect—two sunsets in mere minutes. Later that same night, the Perseid meteor shower will peak, creating a rare celestial convergence.
For Sara Álvarez Rodríguez, born in the village in 1937 and a lifelong resident, the transformation is bittersweet. She remembers when 200 people called Avellanosa home in the 1950s, when fishermen cycled to neighboring towns and the postman's donkey knew the route by heart. Mechanized farming emptied the countryside, sending generations to Madrid and beyond. This story reminds us how the cosmos occasionally turns its spotlight on forgotten corners of our world, inviting us to look up together—and perhaps see our own small places anew.

item.title: Father builds adaptive skateboard for son with cerebral palsy: 'My dream is to provide fun for him'
item.description:
In Cariacica, Brazil, a railway worker named Jonas de Araújo has built a custom skateboard for his son Davi, who is about to turn eleven. The project represents months of careful planning and collaboration with a metalworker, all inspired by a video Jonas saw online of another father doing something similar for his child. What makes this skateboard special is its thoughtful design: an external frame for stability, a handlebar for Davi to grip, and a base where his foot can be secured—features that allow a child with cerebral palsy and low vision to experience the joy of skateboarding.
Davi was born prematurely after his mother contracted toxoplasmosis during pregnancy, an infection that can cause serious complications for unborn babies. He was diagnosed with hydrocephalus at birth and later with cerebral palsy, epilepsy (now controlled), and visual impairment. Despite these challenges, his father describes him as happy, intelligent, and full of life. Davi can respond to verbal commands and perform many daily tasks independently, though he uses a wheelchair for longer distances. The skateboard joins other adaptive equipment Jonas and friends have created, including a modified bicycle and a PVC walker—all designed to give Davi access to ordinary childhood experiences.
This story captures something quietly profound about parenthood and creativity. Jonas speaks of how raising Davi has taught him to find "the extraordinary in the simple," and his homemade skateboard is a testament to that philosophy. It's a reminder that inclusion often begins with imagination and a parent's determination to help their child feel the wind in their hair, just like any other kid.

item.title: Eliza McCartney on her signature smile: 'You convert all the emotions into excitement'
item.description:
New Zealand pole vaulter Eliza McCartney's path to her recent Commonwealth Games gold medal has been anything but straightforward. After winning Olympic bronze at just 19 in Rio, she seemed poised for a dominant decade in her sport, where athletes typically peak in their late twenties. Instead, chronic Achilles issues derailed her trajectory, forcing her to miss competitions and step away for extended periods. Her gold medal victory in Glasgow this year—ten years after that Olympic podium finish—carries profound meaning after nearly a decade of managing expectations, injuries, and self-doubt.
McCartney's struggles haven't been purely physical. She's had to confront an autoimmune response that causes her Achilles tendons to flare unpredictably, making training and competition precarious. Beyond the pain, she's grieved the loss of the career arc she once envisioned and the identity she thought would define her twenties. Through patient work with her team, she's learned to manage her condition well enough to compete, even if her body won't deliver the consistent highs she once anticipated. She's made peace with that reality.
What sets McCartney apart is how she competes: with an unmistakable smile. While many elite athletes channel anger or grit, she's discovered that authenticity works best for her. Stress and pressure make her tense; joy and openness help her jump freely. Converting every emotion—even difficult ones—into excitement has become her signature approach. Her story is a quiet testament to resilience that doesn't look like gritted teeth, and to finding success on your own terms, even when the path looks nothing like you imagined.

item.title: ‘This is what’s working’: Indigenous leaders on environment solutions in their communities
item.description:
To mark the International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples, Mongabay spoke with nine Indigenous leaders across five continents about environmental solutions that are actually working in their communities—and why some well-intentioned efforts fall short. The conversations revealed a crucial gap between top-down conservation strategies and the nuanced, place-based knowledge that Indigenous peoples bring to land stewardship.
Eriberto Guerra's forest garden in the Peruvian Amazon offers a telling example. When government officials promoted agroforestry with coffee or cacao and just one or two companion crops, local farmers found the approach too rigid. Guerra instead cultivates dozens of species alongside traditional plants, creating resilience against crop failure and market fluctuations. His biodiverse garden now attracts endemic birds and wildlife researchers while sustaining his family—a living demonstration of why Indigenous methods often outperform standardized programs. The interviews spanned solutions from reforestation strategies to preserving endemic plants and strengthening traditional governance systems, but a common thread emerged: initiatives succeed when they incorporate local knowledge and fail when they ignore cultural realities.
This collection of voices matters because it challenges assumptions about who holds expertise in conservation. The leaders interviewed—from Malaysia to the Democratic Republic of Congo, from Panama to Brazil—aren't asking for new solutions to be imposed from outside. They're pointing to systems that already work, refined over generations, asking to be heard and supported. In an era of climate urgency, their message is both practical and profound: the most effective environmental strategies may already exist in communities living closest to the land, waiting not to be invented but to be recognized and respected.

item.title: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world
item.description:
As Europe prepares for its first total solar eclipse in over 25 years, a dedicated community of eclipse chasers is converging on the continent's prime viewing locations. For these enthusiasts, witnessing the moon briefly block out the sun isn't a once-in-a-lifetime event—it's part of a passionate pursuit that takes them across the globe.
Mark Griffiths drove two days from Cheshire to Spain's Galicia region, equipped with high-end cameras, a telescope, and a drone. What began as a disappointing trip to see the northern lights in Shetland six years ago evolved into what he candidly calls an addiction—one that now has him leading monthly tours to Iceland. Meanwhile, Samantha and Gregory Phillips-Brown flew from upstate New York to Iceland, booking their trip over a year in advance. They were captivated by their first eclipse in 2023, when daylight vanished and birdsong suddenly ceased. Now they're navigating Facebook groups and monitoring road closures to secure the perfect viewing spot in Iceland's remote Westfjords peninsula, where the path of totality will pass.
What makes this story quietly remarkable is how it captures a very human impulse—the willingness to travel thousands of miles and brave logistical challenges for just a few minutes of cosmic wonder. These eclipse hunters aren't driven by scientific duty but by something more elemental: the desire to stand in the moon's shadow and experience the same awe that must have terrified Iceland's first settlers over a millennium ago, when myth rather than science explained the darkening sky.

item.title: Bilbies released into Qld national park where they were once extinct
item.description:
In the quiet hours before dawn in western Queensland, conservationists are carefully opening hessian bags and watching bilbies bounce back into a landscape they haven't inhabited in more than fifty years. One hundred and fifty of the rabbit-eared marsupials have been released into Currawinya National Park, marking the first time in Queensland that bilbies have been reintroduced to an area where they had become locally extinct since the 1970s.
The journey to this moment has been long and humbling. A predator-proof fence installed in 2003 initially failed when feral cats breached it in 2010, but persistence paid off. Inside the protected area, the bilby population has flourished to around 1,000 individuals, and some adventurous bilbies have already escaped to establish thriving lives beyond the fence. After a decade of preparation and intensive predator control, conditions finally aligned for this careful release into the true wild—no fences, no guarantees, just the hope that these boom-and-bust creatures can reclaim their ancient home.
What makes this story quietly remarkable is not just the technical achievement of reintroduction, but the vision behind it. Conservationists don't want Australia's native species to exist only as museum pieces behind barriers. They dream of a future where tourists might glimpse a bilby bouncing across the bush, where road signs might one day read "Beware of Bilby Crossing." It's a reminder that with patience, collaboration, and a willingness to learn from failure, we can sometimes give back what was lost.

item.title: Grupo Flor Serrana releases album with songs preserving siriri and cururu traditions in Mato Grosso
item.description:
A musical group in Brazil has taken songs passed down through generations and given them a permanent form. Grupo Flor Serrana, founded in 2012 in the rural communities around Cuiabá in Mato Grosso state, has released its first album—a collection of 19 tracks that capture the spirit of two traditional musical styles, siriri and cururu, along with the devotional practices woven into rural life in the region.
The album, "Flor Serrana: as tradições da serra abaixo" (Flor Serrana: the traditions from below the mountains), represents more than a decade of performance by the group, which was started by Helena Maria and Nezinho during traditional saint festivals in their communities. Until now, these songs lived primarily in oral tradition, sung at gatherings and religious celebrations honoring Santo Antônio, São Gonçalo, and Nossa Senhora Aparecida. The recording was made possible through the Gambira Cultural initiative, using funds from the Paulo Gustavo Law administered by Cuiabá's municipal culture office, and is now available on digital platforms.
This story matters because it shows how cultural memory finds new life when communities bridge the gap between oral tradition and modern media. By recording these songs, Grupo Flor Serrana has created a archive of rural identity and religious expression that might otherwise fade as generations pass. It's a quiet act of preservation—taking what has always belonged to gatherings under open skies and ensuring it can travel beyond, reaching ears that might never attend a countryside saint's festival but can still be moved by its music.

item.title: The race is on in a secret location to save one of our rarest orchids
item.description:
In a modest green shed outside Melbourne, volunteers are carefully preparing to plant 500 rosella spider orchids back into the wild — nearly doubling the population of one of Australia's rarest flowers. The rosella spider orchid, found nowhere else on Earth, is critically endangered in Victoria. Research scientist Alex McLachlan and his team at the Royal Botanic Gardens have spent years raising these plants from seed, a painstaking process involving specialized care and countless volunteer hours.
Australian orchids are masters of disguise and survival, spending most of their lives hidden underground and requiring very particular relationships with fungi, soil conditions, and specialized pollinators to thrive. When conditions align, they produce remarkable flowers: some mimic female wasps to attract males, others trap gnats with hinged petals, and the flying duck orchid has evolved blooms that look exactly like a duck in flight. This pickiness makes them both fascinating and vulnerable — more than 200 Australian orchid species are currently at risk of extinction.
This story offers a quiet reminder of the intricate work happening behind the scenes to preserve biodiversity. It reveals the dedication required to save even a single plant species and the remarkable adaptations that make orchids worth protecting. In an era of environmental concern, the patient efforts of scientists and volunteers working with tiny tubers in cold sheds represent hope that careful attention and collective action can make a difference, one flower at a time.

item.title: Madonna pays tribute to 'genius, otherworldly' producer William Orbit
item.description:
The music world is reflecting on the legacy of William Orbit, the acclaimed British producer who died at home on July 23 at age 69. His family announced his passing without specifying a cause, prompting heartfelt tributes from artists whose careers he helped shape. Among the most moving came from Madonna, who credited Orbit with transforming her sound and reigniting her creative spirit in the late 1990s.
Orbit's collaboration with Madonna on the 1998 album *Ray of Light* marked a pivotal moment for both artists. The record blended electronic dance music, ambient techno, pop, and trip-hop into something genuinely new, earning three Grammy Awards and remaining widely regarded as one of Madonna's finest works. In her Instagram tribute, the singer described how Orbit unlocked something previously unrealized in her, inspiring her to sing and write with fresh freedom. She recalled their studio sessions as almost sacred, sitting in silence while waiting for his ideas to emerge from keyboard or guitar. The partnership continued through her 2000 album *Music* and several tracks on 2012's *MDNA*.
Beyond Madonna, Orbit's production work touched an impressive range of artists including Blur, U2, Pink, Britney Spears, and Robbie Williams, cementing his reputation as one of the most versatile and innovative producers of his generation. This story matters not just as news of a loss, but as a reminder of how certain creative partnerships can unlock entirely new artistic possibilities—how one person's singular vision can become the catalyst for another's transformation, leaving music that continues to resonate decades later.

item.title: Where in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse?
item.description:
For the first time since 1999, skywatchers across the UK will witness an almost total solar eclipse on a Wednesday evening in August, with the moon blocking between 88% and 96% of the sun's light. It's a rare celestial event—the next comparable viewing won't occur until 2081, making this a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for many.
The western regions of the UK will enjoy the most dramatic views, with Plymouth seeing 95% coverage, followed by Cardiff and Belfast at just over 93%. Even cities farther east, like London and Edinburgh, will experience coverage above 90%. Astronomers recommend finding elevated spots with clear western horizons—places like Parliament Hill in London or similar vantage points elsewhere. Because it's happening in August, there's a better-than-usual chance of clear skies, though Scotland and Northern Ireland may face cloud cover. Scotland's astronomer royal suggests monitoring weather forecasts closely and being ready to travel to cloud-free areas for the best experience.
Safety is paramount: looking directly at the partially eclipsed sun can cause serious, painless retinal damage. Following the 1999 eclipse, about 70 people reported vision problems. Experts urge using certified eclipse glasses that meet international safety standards, or indirect viewing methods like pinhole projectors. This celestial phenomenon offers a chance to witness the intricate dance between Earth, moon, and sun—a reminder of the cosmos unfolding above us, visible to anyone who takes a moment to look up safely.

item.title: Baker Boy wins big at NIMAs
item.description:
The National Indigenous Music Awards (NIMAs) celebrated a vibrant cross-section of Australian Indigenous artistry, with Yolŋu hip hop artist Baker Boy emerging as a standout winner. His album *Djandjay*, dedicated to his grandmother who introduced hip hop to Arnhem Land after a Los Angeles honeymoon, claimed Album of the Year. The record marks an artistic evolution for Baker Boy, moving beyond his earlier "Fresh Prince of Arnhem Land" persona to tackle weightier themes including the voice referendum, impostor syndrome, and systemic racism with grungier, more introspective sounds.
