His track "Thick Skin," featuring Thelma Plum, Emma Donovan, Kee'ahn, and Jada Weaze, swept both Song of the Year and Film Clip of the Year.
The evening's top honour, Artist of the Year, went to Butchulla duo Birdz and Fred Leone, whose collaborative EP *GIRA* blends hip hop with traditional songman elements. The awards also recognized enduring contributions to Indigenous music, inducting Queensland jazz and blues artist Marlene Cummins and Galiwin'ku's Saltwater Band into the NIMAs Hall of Fame. Remote communities featured prominently: Terry Guyula, performing as Drifting Clouds and describing himself as "the most chill band from Arnhem Land," won Best New Talent, while Bulman School earned the Indigenous Language Award for a song exploring Dreamtime stories.
This story offers a window into the depth and diversity of Indigenous Australian music—a landscape where hip hop meets traditional songlines, where remote community schools preserve ancient stories through contemporary sound, and where family legacies continue to shape new artistic frontiers.

item.title: Elderly woman dances after final chemotherapy and rolls out red carpet to honor medical team: 'I am happy and so are they'
item.description:
When 81-year-old Irene Rodrigues de Lara completed her final chemotherapy session, she didn't simply walk out of the hospital — she danced. On a Monday morning in Sorocaba, Brazil, Irene celebrated her cancer recovery by rolling out a red carpet for the medical team who treated her, complete with a thank-you banner and a joyful dance to one of her favorite songs. Her daughter captured the moment on video, which quickly spread beyond the family, touching viewers with its exuberant gratitude.
Irene's journey through eight months of treatment for intestinal cancer wasn't without fear. A niece had recently died from the same disease, and at first Irene hesitated to begin treatment. But she found strength in her own nature. "I'm not a sad person," she explained. "I'm happy, I like to sing and dance. That gave me the strength." Her family knows cancer's weight intimately — both her children have faced the disease, and a brother was undergoing treatment at another hospital during Irene's own chemotherapy. Yet they've chosen to meet each milestone with celebration rather than dread.
What makes this story quietly remarkable is its insistence on joy in the face of difficulty. Irene's red-carpet tribute wasn't just about marking the end of treatment; it was about honoring the human connections that sustained her — the caring nurses, the doctors who became friends, even the kind doorman. Now declared on track for recovery, Irene is already looking ahead, planning to reach 107 years old as one of her doctors playfully predicted. It's a reminder that how we move through hardship matters as much as the outcome itself.

item.title: From small cats to pangolins: Detection dogs help track elusive species
item.description:
In South Africa's Karoo region, specially trained detection dogs are revolutionizing how scientists study some of the world's most elusive animals. Conservation biologist Michelle Marie Schroeder works with two German Shorthaired Pointers, Lyka and Sebala, who can locate animal droppings by scent—a skill that has transformed her research on the secretive black-footed cat. While Schroeder found only four scat samples in over a year of searching on her own, ten-year-old Lyka has discovered hundreds in just months.
The black-footed cat presents unique tracking challenges. Unlike other carnivores that leave droppings in predictable locations to mark territory, these small felines scatter their scat seemingly at random—inside burrows, beneath shrubs, in hidden spots. Each sample, though, contains what Schroeder calls "little nuggets of genetic data" that reveal an animal's sex, individual identity, diet, parasites, and genetic connections to other populations. Early findings are encouraging: samples from sites 700 kilometers apart show healthy genetic diversity and evidence that cats can still move and interbreed across the landscape, though researchers caution this represents only a small portion of the region. The dogs' abilities extend beyond cats—Schroeder has launched a pilot project using them to track the equally cryptic Temminck's pangolin, with plans to build a DNA database that could help trace illegally trafficked pangolin scales back to their origins.
This story quietly illustrates how an ancient partnership—humans and dogs—continues to unlock new scientific possibilities, allowing researchers to study rare animals without traps or collars while uncovering crucial conservation insights one discovered sample at a time.

item.title: How can landscape recover after devastating fires?
item.description:
Grassfires sweeping through the UK are leaving conservationists facing a sobering reality: what takes hours to destroy can require decades to restore. Recent blazes have scorched nature reserves, farmland, and protected countryside from the West Midlands to Scotland, devastating carefully nurtured habitats and the intricate webs of life they support.
The damage ripples through ecosystems in cascading waves. When flames consume grasses, wildflowers, and trees, they eliminate the food sources that invertebrates depend on, which in turn affects the birds and mammals higher up the food chain. At Portway Hill in the West Midlands, a rare colony of marbled white butterflies lost the plants they relied on. At Cannock Chase, fires killed adders and toads. In Scotland's Cairngorms, roughly ten square miles of moorland burned, destroying insects, reptiles, lichens, and mosses at an RSPB reserve. Staffordshire alone saw about 600 outdoor fires in July—double the previous year's count.
Yet conservationists haven't given up. Restoration is possible, though painstakingly slow, involving careful reseeding of meadows and strategic tree planting. Some forward-thinking projects are building resilience into the landscape itself: native broadleaf trees create cooler, less flammable woodlands, while restored wetlands keep surrounding areas damp. Sphagnum moss at The Roaches helped protect ground from severe damage during a June fire. This story matters because it reveals both our vulnerability and our capacity to adapt—a quiet reminder that nature's recovery, like its destruction, unfolds on its own patient timeline.

item.title: 'If it weren't for him, a tragedy could have happened': pitbull faces mountain lion inside home and protects family in São Paulo condominium
item.description:
In the early hours of a Thursday morning in São Paulo's Serra da Cantareira, a pitbull named Ragnar may have prevented a tragedy when he confronted a mountain lion that had entered his family's home. The household includes three young children, the youngest just three months old. Mirella Ramos, the children's mother, had risen around 3 a.m. to nurse her infant when Ragnar suddenly bolted toward the back corridor, sensing danger before any human knew what was happening.
What followed was an intense struggle at the backdoor between the family dog and an adult puma. The family had left the back door slightly ajar, as they often did in their gated community, allowing Ragnar to go outside. While residents had occasionally spotted wildlife in the area, no one anticipated such a direct encounter. The fight only ended when the couple's three-year-old daughter began crying and calling for the dog, prompting Ragnar to disengage and retreat into the house for emergency care. He sustained severe injuries, including facial lacerations and damage to a vein near his heart, requiring immediate surgery.
This story offers a glimpse into the increasingly blurred boundaries between urban development and wild habitats, even in major metropolitan areas. It's a reminder that wildlife corridors persist in unexpected places, and that the animals sharing our landscapes—both domestic and wild—navigate risks we rarely see. Ragnar's instinctive protection of his family, at great personal cost, quietly underscores the deep bonds between humans and their animal companions, and raises thoughtful questions about coexistence in spaces where nature and civilization overlap.
